Volterra's Function

Differentiable everywhere with a bounded derivative, yet that derivative is not Riemann integrable. Bumps rise over a fat Cantor set.

The function itself joins up smoothly. The trouble is its derivative, oscillating hard on a thick set. Riemann sums cannot capture that oscillation.

For example, measure the slope of a smooth road with a 📏 ruler, but the reading jumps wherever the ruler touches. The road is fine; the measurement fails.

Finally we cite Lebesgue's criterion as a theorem (its proof is measure theory, so we keep it at idea level — see the measure/lebesgue scenes): a bounded function on [a,b][a,b][a,b] is Riemann integrable iff it is continuous almost everywhere, i.e. its discontinuity set has Lebesgue measure 000.

    Here f′f'f′ is bounded (Problem 2), its discontinuity set contains CCC, and CCC is closed with measure 1/21/21/2 (the complement's total length is lim⁡N→∞1−2−N2=12\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1-2^{-N}}{2} = \frac12limN→∞​21−2−N​=21​). A discontinuity set of positive measure means f′f'f′ is not Riemann integrable.

    The punchline: a function can be differentiable everywhere with bounded derivative, yet its derivative need not be Riemann integrable.
